digest.top_line: STAMPEDE, high-risk non-metastatic prostate: 2yr abiraterone ± enzalutamide + ADT → MFS HR 0.53 (0.44-0.64), OS HR 0.60 (0.48-0.73); enzalutamide adds nothing.
digest.tldr: Prostate carries the day: pooled STAMPEDE IPD in high-risk non-metastatic disease shows 6-yr OS 86% vs 77% adding 2yr abiraterone to ADT. MFS benefit held whether RT was planned (HR 0.54) or not (HR 0.51); 85% planned RT. Abi+enza arm: grade 3+ AEs 58% vs 32%, with no extra MFS benefit.

sites.intro: RT-backbone population: 85% planned prostate RT (74 Gy/37 fx or hypofractionated equivalent), mandated for N0.

studies.name: STAMPEDE abiraterone ± enzalutamide in high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer (meta-analysis)
studies.tldr: MFS HR 0.53 (0.44-0.64) and OS HR 0.60 (0.48-0.73) adding 2yr abiraterone ± enzalutamide to ADT in high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer.

details.text: 📊 Efficacy, combination therapy vs ADT alone (pooled IPD)

details: 💊 Adding enzalutamide gave no extra MFS benefit: interaction HR 1.02 (0.70-1.50), p=0.91
🔍 RT per local guidelines: 74 Gy/37 fx to prostate + SVs or hypofractionated equivalent
🔍 RT mandated for N0, encouraged for N+; 1684 (85%) planned RT
⚠️ Grade 5 AEs: 0 control, 3 abiraterone, 4 abiraterone + enzalutamide
⚠️ Primary endpoint switched from OS to MFS, prespecified before inspecting efficacy by arm
⚠️ Open-label; controls could get 2nd-gen hormonal agents for nmCRPC, which would bias OS toward null

verdict.rationale: Pooled IPD from two randomised phase 3 trials, 72-mo f/u, with both MFS and OS improved. The OS→MFS switch was prespecified before efficacy was seen. Authors call it a new standard.
verdict.audience: High-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer (N+ or high-risk N0) starting ADT

studies.significance: The MFS benefit held whether or not RT was planned: HR 0.54 (0.44-0.67) with RT vs 0.51 (0.34-0.76) without, interaction p=0.67. So abiraterone adds to prostate RT and does not stand in for it. The RT was 74 Gy/37 fx to prostate + SVs, and the source does not describe pelvic nodal fields for the 39% who were N+.
studies.monday_clinic: In N+ or high-risk N0 non-metastatic prostate cancer starting long-course ADT with prostate RT, this supports 2 yr of abiraterone + prednisolone without enzalutamide. It does not extend to men treated with prostatectomy, who were not studied.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prespecified IPD **meta-analysis of two open-label, randomised (1:1) phase 3 trials** in the STAMPEDE platform, run at 113 UK and Swiss sites. N=1974, randomised 2011-2016, with no overlapping controls. Median follow-up was **72 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **High-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer** on conventional imaging: N+, or N0 with at least two of T3/T4, Gleason 8-10, or PSA ≥40 ng/mL. Pts relapsing with high-risk features were also eligible. Median age was 68, and 774 (39%) were node-positive. Clinically significant cardiovascular disease was excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: All pts received **3 yr ADT**. The combination arm added abiraterone 1000 mg + prednisolone 5 mg daily for **2 yr**, and the second trial also added enzalutamide 160 mg. If RT was omitted, treatment could continue until progression.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Per local guidelines: **74 Gy/37 fx to prostate + SVs** or a hypofractionated equivalent. RT was **mandated for N0** and encouraged for N+. RT was planned in 85% overall: 99% of N0, 71% of N+ and 7% of previously treated pts.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: MFS**, which was changed from OS before any efficacy inspection and approved by the steering committee on Dec 2, 2019. Secondary endpoints were OS, prostate cancer-specific survival, biochemical failure-free survival, PFS and toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Both trials showed the benefit on their own: MFS HR 0.54 in the abiraterone trial and 0.53 in the abiraterone + enzalutamide trial, with no between-trial heterogeneity (I² p=0.90).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Grade 3+ AEs in the first 24 mo were **37% vs 29%** in the abiraterone trial and **58% vs 32%** in the abiraterone + enzalutamide trial. The main drivers were hypertension and ALT elevation. There were 7 grade 5 events, all in the combination arms.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The backbone is long-course ADT with prostate RT, which the authors frame as standard for this population. Adding enzalutamide to abiraterone also gave no extra benefit here, consistent with the modest rPFS gains and absent OS benefit the authors cite from that combination in mCRPC.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with high-risk N0 or N+ non-metastatic prostate cancer on conventional imaging who are starting long-course ADT, mostly with prostate RT. Does not represent men treated with prostatectomy, and relapse after prior local therapy is underrepresented.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Staging used conventional imaging only. Toxicity was reported only for the first 2 yr, and data on subsequent therapy are unreliable. Heterogeneity by PS 1-2 (HR 0.86, 0.58-1.28) makes the benefit less certain in less fit men.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Abiraterone intensification improved MFS and OS on top of ADT whether or not RT was planned. **Enzalutamide added toxicity without extra efficacy.** Open questions are the right duration, the benefit after prostatectomy, and the benefit in PSMA-staged disease, none of which were tested.

studies.interpretation:
The main message for a radiation oncologist is that abiraterone works on top of the local therapy, not instead of it. RT was planned in 85% of pts and mandated for node-negative disease, so the pooled population is largely men getting prostate RT with 3 years of ADT. The prespecified subgroup split by planned RT gives nearly identical MFS hazard ratios (0.54 with RT, 0.51 without, interaction p=0.67). That argues against reading systemic intensification as a replacement for RT or as a reason to shorten ADT. The trial did not test either of those, and the backbone stayed fixed.

The primary endpoint change deserves scrutiny because it is the obvious line of attack. The trial group moved the non-metastatic primary from OS to MFS and pooled the two trials. The authors say this was decided before any efficacy was inspected by arm and was published as a declaration beforehand, which removes most of the concern about outcome switching. It also turns out not to matter much, because OS improved as well (HR 0.60, 6-yr 86% vs 77%). A surrogate-only result would have faced the usual question of whether MFS predicts survival. This one does not have to rely on that argument.

The enzalutamide comparison is indirect: the interaction HR was 1.02 across two separately randomised trials, not a head-to-head test. The confidence interval (0.70-1.50) cannot rule out a small benefit, as the authors say. But grade 3+ AEs nearly doubled in the enzalutamide trial versus its control, so the toxicity cost is clear. For practice this is a de-escalation read: abiraterone + prednisolone, not the doublet.

Three points should temper how far the reader extends this. First, staging was conventional imaging. A population restaged on PSMA-PET would move some of these men into oligometastatic categories, and the effect size in that more selected group is unknown. Second, the pelvic RT volume for node-positive men is not described in the source. Only 71% of N+ men had RT planned at all, so the N+ subgroup result (HR 0.49) is not a clean answer on nodal RT combined with intensification. Third, the performance status interaction (HR 0.86 in PS 1-2) and the unexplained NSAID/aspirin interaction are both fragile subgroup findings. The authors advise against acting on the latter. The former is a reasonable prompt to weigh competing mortality in older or comorbid men.

The open-label design matters more for OS than it might seem. Control pts could receive second-generation hormonal therapy for non-metastatic castration-resistant disease, either on trial or, after 2019, as standard care. That would pull the OS estimate toward the null, so the survival benefit is more likely understated than overstated. Data on subsequent therapy were unreliable, so this cannot be checked.

The decision this moves is systemic intensification alongside definitive RT for high-risk N0 and N+ disease. The questions it leaves open are the benefit after prostatectomy, the optimal duration beyond the pragmatic 2 years, and the benefit in men relapsing after prior local therapy, who were underrepresented.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The abiraterone benefit is independent of planned RT (MFS HR 0.54 with vs 0.51 without, interaction p=0.67), and RT was mandated for N0. It stacks on 74 Gy/37 fx to prostate + SVs with 3 yr ADT. The source does not describe pelvic nodal fields, and only 71% of N+ pts had RT planned.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Two years of abiraterone + prednisolone added to 3 yr ADT improved OS (HR 0.60). Adding enzalutamide gave no extra MFS benefit (interaction HR 1.02) and raised grade 3+ AEs to 58% vs 32%. Enzalutamide adds cost and toxicity without added efficacy.
